authoredSolutions.26:
Break each solution into solute and solvent.

100 g of 98% (w/w) acid: \(98\) g \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) and \(2\) g water.
100 g of 49% (w/w) acid: \(49\) g \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) and \(51\) g water.

After mixing:
mass of \(H_{2}SO_{4} = 98 + 49 = 147\) g, and \(M(H_{2}SO_{4}) = 98\) g mol\(^{-1}\), so \(n_{acid} = 147/98 = 1.5\) mol.
mass of water \(= 2 + 51 = 53\) g, so \(n_{water} = 53/18 = 2.944\) mol.

Mole fraction of the acid:
\(x = \dfrac{1.5}{1.5 + 2.944} = \dfrac{1.5}{4.444} = 0.3375 \approx 0.337\).

Hence the mole fraction of \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) is \(0.337\) (option C). Note \(0.663\) is the mole fraction of water, not of the acid.

The figure shows \(1,1\)-dibromobutane, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CHBr_{2}\). A geminal dihalide with \(2\) equivalents of \(NaNH_{2}\) undergoes double dehydrohalogenation:

\(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CHBr_{2} + 2NaNH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}C \equiv CH\) (but-1-yne) \(= X\).

But-1-yne is a terminal alkyne, so \(NaNH_{2}\) removes the acidic \(\equiv C-H\) to give the sodium acetylide, which is then alkylated by the isopropyl bromide:

\(CH_{3}CH_{2}C \equiv C^{-}Na^{+} + (CH_{3})_{2}CHBr \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}C \equiv C-CH(CH_{3})_{2}\).

Numbering the six-carbon chain so the triple bond and then the substituent get the lowest locants gives \(2\)-methylhex-\(3\)-yne, i.e. option C.

Configurations: \(Cr = [Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}\), \(Mn = [Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}\).

Statement-I: the first electron is removed from the singly occupied \(4s\) of Cr but from a paired \(4s^{2}\) of Mn, and Cr\(^{+}\) attains the stable \(3d^{5}\) configuration. Hence \(IE_{1}(Cr) = 653\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\) is lower than \(IE_{1}(Mn) = 717\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\). Statement-I is TRUE.

Arrhenius: \(k = Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}\), i.e. \(\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_{a}}{2.303RT}\).

(A) FALSE. The Boltzmann factor \(e^{-E_{a}/RT}\) is the fraction of molecules whose kinetic energy is EQUAL TO OR GREATER THAN \(E_{a}\), not less than \(E_{a}\).

(B) TRUE. At fixed \(T\), a smaller \(E_{a}\) makes \(e^{-E_{a}/RT}\) larger, so \(k\) is larger and the reaction is faster.

(C) TRUE. This is the standard temperature-coefficient rule of thumb: a rise of about \(10^{\circ}C\) roughly doubles the rate for many reactions near room temperature.

(D) FALSE. A plot of \(\log k\) versus \(1/T\) is linear with slope \(-\dfrac{E_{a}}{2.303R}\); the slope is \(-E_{a}/R\) only for \(\ln k\) versus \(1/T\).

Correct: B and C only, option D.

Reactions of glucose:

(A) with hydroxylamine \(NH_{2}OH\), the aldehyde group condenses to the oxime, glucose oxime (glucoxime) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

(B) with bromine water, a mild oxidant, only the \(-CHO\) is oxidised to \(-COOH\) giving gluconic acid \(\rightarrow\) (I).

(C) with excess acetic anhydride, all five \(-OH\) groups are acetylated giving glucose pentaacetate \(\rightarrow\) (II).

(D) with concentrated \(HNO_{3}\), a strong oxidant, both the \(-CHO\) and the terminal \(-CH_{2}OH\) are oxidised to \(-COOH\) giving the dicarboxylic saccharic (glucaric) acid \(\rightarrow\) (III).

A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III: option B.

Approximate dipole moments: \(H_{2}O\) \(1.85\) D, \(NH_{3}\) \(1.47\) D, \(CHCl_{3}\) \(1.04\) D, \(H_{2}S\) \(0.97\) D, \(NF_{3}\) \(0.24\) D.

\(NF_{3}\) has the lowest value: it is pyramidal like \(NH_{3}\), but the highly electronegative F atoms pull the bond moments AWAY from N, opposing the lone-pair moment, so the two contributions largely cancel (in \(NH_{3}\) they reinforce). Hence \(X = NF_{3}\).

Nitrogen in \(NF_{3}\) has \(5\) valence electrons, three of which are used in \(N-F\) bonds, leaving one lone pair.

Statement-I: first ionization enthalpies (kJ mol\(^{-1}\)) are \(C = 1086\), \(O = 1314\), \(N = 1402\), \(F = 1681\). Oxygen falls below nitrogen because removing one electron from \(2p^{4}\) relieves inter-electronic repulsion in the doubly occupied orbital and leaves the stable half-filled \(2p^{3}\). Hence \(C < O < N < F\) is correct. Statement-I is TRUE.

Statement-II: magnitudes of electron gain enthalpy (kJ mol\(^{-1}\)) are \(S \approx 200\), \(Se \approx 195\), \(Te \approx 190\), \(Po \approx 174\), \(O \approx 141\). For a basic buffer, \(pK_{a}(NH_{4}^{+}) = 14 - pK_{b}(NH_{4}OH) = 14 - 4.75 = 9.25\).

Henderson equation: \(pH = pK_{a} + \log\dfrac{[NH_{3}]}{[NH_{4}^{+}]}\).

\(pH = 9.25\) requires \([NH_{3}] = [NH_{4}^{+}]\), i.e. exactly half the base must be neutralised, so \(n(NH_{4}OH) = 2 \times n(HCl)\).

(A) \(n_{base} = 0.2 \times 0.4 = 0.08\), \(n_{acid} = 0.1 \times 1 = 0.10\): acid is in excess, no buffer.
(B) \(n_{base} = 0.2 \times 0.5 = 0.10\), \(n_{acid} = 0.1 \times 0.5 = 0.05\): base left \(= 0.05\), salt formed \(= 0.05\), ratio \(= 1\), so \(pH = 9.25\). CORRECT.
(C) \(n_{base} = 0.5 \times 0.2 = 0.10\), \(n_{acid} = 0.2 \times 0.5 = 0.10\): complete neutralisation to \(NH_{4}Cl\), an acidic salt solution, not a buffer.
(D) \(n_{base} = 0.4 \times 1 = 0.40\), \(n_{acid} = 0.1 \times 1 = 0.10\): ratio \(= 0.30/0.10 = 3\), \(pH = 9.25 + \log 3 = 9.73\).

Answer B.

Balmer series has \(n_{2} = 2\). The first (lowest-energy) Balmer line is \(n = 3 \rightarrow 2\) and the second is \(n = 4 \rightarrow 2\).

\(E \propto \left(\dfrac{1}{2^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n^{2}}\right)\).

First line: \(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{5}{36} = 0.1389\), and this equals \(x\).
Second line: \(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{3}{16} = 0.1875\).

Ratio \(= \dfrac{0.1875}{0.1389} = 1.35\).

Hence the second Balmer line has energy \(1.35x\) J, option D.

Requirements of a primary standard:

(A) TRUE. Stable hydrated salts of definite composition are routinely used as primary standards, e.g. oxalic acid dihydrate \(H_{2}C_{2}O_{4} \cdot 2H_{2}O\) and Mohr's salt \(FeSO_{4}(NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4} \cdot 6H_{2}O\).

(B) TRUE. It must be unaffected by air, i.e. non-hygroscopic, non-efflorescent and not oxidised by \(O_{2}\) or attacked by \(CO_{2}\), so its mass and composition do not drift while weighing.

(C) TRUE. Its reaction in the titration must be rapid (instantaneous) and follow a single known stoichiometry so the end point is sharp.

(D) FALSE. A primary standard must be readily SOLUBLE in the titration solvent (normally water) so a solution of exactly known concentration can be prepared.

(E) FALSE. It should have a HIGH relative molar mass, so that a large mass is weighed out and the relative weighing error is small.

Correct: A, B and C only, option B.

\(Ni\) in \([Ni(PPh_{3})_{2}Cl_{2}]\) is \(Ni^{2+}\), \(3d^{8}\). \(PPh_{3}\) is bulky and weak-field, so the complex is TETRAHEDRAL (\(sp^{3}\)) with two unpaired electrons, which is why it is paramagnetic. (The square-planar \(dsp^{2}\) form would be diamagnetic.)

(A) INCORRECT. A tetrahedral \(MA_{2}B_{2}\) complex cannot show geometrical isomerism, because all four positions in a tetrahedron are adjacent to one another; cis/trans exists only for square-planar or octahedral geometries.

(B) INCORRECT. Tetrahedral \(Ni^{2+}\) is a \(d^{8}\) ion with a partly filled d shell, so d-d transitions occur and the complex is coloured (blue-green), not white.

(C) CORRECT. \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{2 \times 4} = \sqrt{8} = 2.83 \approx 2.84\) BM.

(D) INCORRECT. For a tetrahedral \(d^{8}\) ion the filling is \(e^{4}t_{2}^{4}\), giving CFSE \(= 4(-0.6\Delta_{t}) + 4(+0.4\Delta_{t}) = -0.8\Delta_{t}\). The value is expressed in \(\Delta_{t}\), not \(\Delta_{0}\); since \(\Delta_{t} = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_{0}\), this is \(-0.36\Delta_{0}\), so the quoted \(-0.8\Delta_{0}\) is wrong.

(E) CORRECT. \(Ni(CO)_{4}\) is tetrahedral, and so is this complex, so the geometrical arrangement is indeed similar.

Incorrect statements: A, B and D only, option B.

A good reducing agent is easily oxidised, so the SMALLER (more negative) the standard reduction potential of its couple, the stronger it is as a reducing agent.

The reduced member of each couple is the potential reducing agent:
\(Al\) from \(Al^{3+}/Al\), \(E^{\circ} = -1.66\) V
\(Cr\) from \(Cr^{3+}/Cr\), \(E^{\circ} = -0.74\) V
\(Fe^{2+}\) from \(Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}\), \(E^{\circ} = +0.77\) V
\(Co^{2+}\) from \(Co^{3+}/Co^{2+}\), \(E^{\circ} = +1.81\) V

Arranging in increasing \(E^{\circ}\) gives decreasing reducing power:
\(Al > Cr > Fe^{2+} > Co^{2+}\).

Option A.
authoredSolutions.43:
Two clues fix A.

(i) A gives a substituted BENZYL ALCOHOL with concentrated NaOH. That is the Cannizzaro reaction, which requires an aldehyde with NO \(\alpha\)-hydrogen; the aldehyde is disproportionated to the corresponding alcohol plus the salt of the acid. So A is an aromatic aldehyde \(Ar-CHO\).

(ii) A undergoes cross-aldol condensation with acetophenone to give a SINGLE product, again consistent with A having no \(\alpha\)-H, so only acetophenone can supply the enolate.

Now apply the molecular formula \(C_{8}H_{8}O_{2}\):
4-methoxybenzaldehyde, \(CH_{3}O-C_{6}H_{4}-CHO\), is \(C_{8}H_{8}O_{2}\) and has no \(\alpha\)-H. With NaOH it gives 4-methoxybenzyl alcohol, a substituted benzyl alcohol. This fits both clues.

Option A (2-hydroxyacetophenone) is a ketone with \(\alpha\)-H, so no Cannizzaro. Option C (4-hydroxybenzaldehyde) is \(C_{7}H_{6}O_{2}\), the wrong formula. Option D is an acid and undergoes neither reaction.

Answer B.

Target: 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, \((CH_{3})_{3}C-CH(OH)-CH_{3}\), a \(C_{6}\) secondary alcohol with an intact tert-butyl group.

(A) WORKS. \((CH_{3})_{3}C-CHO\) with \(CH_{3}MgBr\) then \(H_{3}O^{+}\) adds a methyl to the carbonyl carbon giving \((CH_{3})_{3}C-CH(OH)-CH_{3}\).

(B) FAILS. The alkene drawn is \(CH_{3}CH_{2}-C(CH_{3})_{2}-CH=CH_{2}\) (3,3-dimethylpent-1-ene), a \(C_{7}\) skeleton, so it cannot give a \(C_{6}\) alcohol at all. Independently, \(H_{2}O/H^{+}\) adds by Markovnikov through a SECONDARY carbocation which promptly undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to the more stable tertiary cation, so the product is a rearranged tertiary alcohol.

(C) WORKS. The tetrasubstituted alkene \((CH_{3})_{3}C-C(CH_{3})=C(CH_{3})-C(CH_{3})_{3}\) on reductive ozonolysis \((O_{3}/Zn-H_{2}O)\) is cleaved into two molecules of \((CH_{3})_{3}C-CO-CH_{3}\) (pinacolone), and \(NaBH_{4}/MeOH\) reduces this ketone to \((CH_{3})_{3}C-CH(OH)-CH_{3}\).

(D) WORKS. Pinacolone \((CH_{3})_{3}C-CO-CH_{3}\) with \(LiAlH_{4}\) then \(H_{3}O^{+}\) is reduced directly to the required secondary alcohol.

(E) FAILS. \((CH_{3})_{3}C-C \equiv CH\) with \(H_{2}O/Hg^{2+}/H^{+}\) undergoes Markovnikov hydration to an enol that tautomerises to the KETONE \((CH_{3})_{3}C-CO-CH_{3}\); the reaction stops at pinacolone and does not give an alcohol.

Cannot be prepared by B and E only, option B.

Work backwards. \([R]\) gives a positive iodoform test but a negative Tollens test, so \([R]\) is a METHYL KETONE (\(CH_{3}CO-\)) and not an aldehyde. \([R]\) is obtained from \([Q]\) by \(HgSO_{4}/dil. H_{2}SO_{4}\), which is Markovnikov hydration of an alkyne; a TERMINAL alkyne \(R-C \equiv CH\) hydrates to \(R-CO-CH_{3}\). Hence \([Q]\) is a terminal alkyne.

\([Q]\) comes from \([P]\) (\(C_{9}H_{10}Br_{2}\)) with excess sodamide, i.e. double dehydrohalogenation, which requires the two bromines to be geminal or vicinal on the two carbons that become the triple bond.

Option C, \(4\text{-}CH_{3}C_{6}H_{4}-CBr_{2}-CH_{3}\), is a geminal dibromide of the right formula \(C_{9}H_{10}Br_{2}\). Excess \(NaNH_{2}\) removes both \(HBr\) to give \(4\text{-}CH_{3}C_{6}H_{4}-C \equiv CH\) (4-methylphenylacetylene) \(= [Q]\), a terminal alkyne. Hydration then gives \(4\text{-}CH_{3}C_{6}H_{4}-CO-CH_{3}\) (4-methylacetophenone) \(= [R]\), a methyl ketone: iodoform positive, Tollens negative.

The others fail: option A has its two bromines on two different benzylic carbons (no alkyne possible); option B, \(C_{6}H_{5}-CBr(CH_{3})-CH_{2}Br\), cannot form a triple bond because the brominated carbon also carries phenyl and methyl; option D already contains the bromines on a vinylic unit of a non-aromatic ring and does not lead to the required terminal alkyne.

Answer C.
authoredSolutions.46:
Anode reaction (oxidation of water): \(2H_{2}O \rightarrow O_{2} + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-}\).

Write the anode couple as a reduction and apply the Nernst equation with \(p_{O_{2}} = 1\) bar:

\(E_{O_{2}/H_{2}O} = 1.23 - \dfrac{0.059}{4}\log\dfrac{1}{p_{O_{2}}[H^{+}]^{4}} = 1.23 + 0.059\log[H^{+}] = 1.23 - 0.059\,pH\).

Cathode: \(M^{2+}(1.0\,M) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow M\), \(E = E^{\circ} = 0.994\) V.

\(E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode} = 0.994 - (1.23 - 0.059\,pH) = -0.236 + 0.059\,pH\).

Oxygen starts to evolve when the cell reaction becomes spontaneous, \(E_{cell} \geq 0\):

\(0.059\,pH \geq 0.236 \Rightarrow pH \geq \dfrac{0.236}{0.059} = 4\).

Hence the required pH is \(4\).

A mixed oxide contains the SAME metal in two different oxidation states.

\(Ti_{2}O_{3}\): Ti is \(+3\) only. Not mixed.
\(V_{2}O_{4}\) (i.e. \(VO_{2}\)): V is \(+4\) only. Not mixed.
\(Cr_{2}O_{3}\): Cr is \(+3\) only. Not mixed.
\(Mn_{3}O_{4}\): \(MnO \cdot Mn_{2}O_{3}\), Mn is \(+2\) and \(+3\). MIXED.
\(Fe_{3}O_{4}\): \(FeO \cdot Fe_{2}O_{3}\), Fe is \(+2\) and \(+3\). MIXED.
\(Fe_{2}O_{3}\): Fe is \(+3\) only. Not mixed.
\(Co_{3}O_{4}\): \(CoO \cdot Co_{2}O_{3}\), Co is \(+2\) and \(+3\). MIXED.

Number of mixed oxides \(= 3\).

Comparing with the given \(\log_{10}k = 14.34 - \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{4}}{T/K}\):

\(\dfrac{E_{a1}}{2.303\,R} = 1.5 \times 10^{4}\,K\)

\(E_{a1} = 1.5 \times 10^{4} \times 2.303 \times 8.314 = 2.872 \times 10^{5}\) J mol\(^{-1}\) \(= 287.2\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\).

Given \(E_{a2} = \dfrac{1}{5}E_{a1}\):

\(E_{a2} = \dfrac{287.2}{5} = 57.4\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\) \(\approx 57\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\).
